utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. I believe the Prosecution wants to raise some issues before we move into hearing evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this time it's not me; it's Mr. Milovancevic who has something to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Whiting. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should only like to briefly inform the Trial Chamber, in connection with the obligations that we have undertaken, namely as regards the reduction of time, we have done that, and it has been submitted to the secretary of our schedule, and that is by the end of the day it shall also be submitted to the Trial Chamber. Secondly, I undertook, on Friday, to inform the Trial Chamber of the stage of the translation of the expert's reports. As regards the military expert, according to the official information received from the translation service, the translation should have been finished today, but it will be delayed for a couple of days. As regards the translation of the expert report by Professor Anramov, that one should be finished by the beginning of next week. That is as far as these issues raised on Friday are concerned. The Defence also has been enjoined by the Trial Chamber how to act in connection with the testimony of Milan Babic. We are to submit a submission in respect of those parts that we failed to cross-examine, and that deadline expires on Thursday, as well as for the rebuttal evidence. As we have quite a condensed schedule now with witnesses, we are asking the Chamber if that is at all possible, to extend this deadline for us until next Monday, instead of this Thursday. If that is at all possible. That would be all from the Defence team. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. And thank you specifically for the filing that you say you are now going to be making today. I perhaps was remiss in emphasising to you the need, when preparing that filing, to give serious thought to the use of 92 bis and 89(F), because I can assure you, without the use of those two Rules, it's going to be virtually impossible to fit in within the 158 hours, but if you make extensive use of them, particularly with witnesses who are talking about similar evidence, or who are not talking about anything that the accused -- personally may have done, it will be very helpful. Then you will be able to fit in very smoothly within that time period. As to the translations relating to the two reports, I think I will have to defer to the Prosecution here, because they are the people who are eagerly awaiting those reports and they need to prepare. How does this affect you, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. What has been stated by Defence counsel is fine. We will receive the reports and there will be adequate time for us to consider them and respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. The Babic evidence, I must confess, I have not given much thought to what you have raised, Mr. Milovancevic, since the decision of that Appeals Chamber was handed down. I'm not quite sure one has to look at the decision that we had made as to look at whether or not your time has not run and expired from the time the order was made or whether it can still run now, after the Appeals Chamber decision. And you are saying, if it is running from now, from the date of that Appeals Chamber's decision, it expires on Thursday but you need an extension. I really need to confer with my colleagues outside court and look at the document itself to be able to say whether or not you still have time, that can still be extended.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just could state our position on this issue. In the event the Trial Chamber finds that there is time still to extend, that it can still be extended, and therefore considers the request from the Defence for an extension from the deadline of Thursday, the 21st of September until Monday the 25th of September, we have no opposition to that request. And I can certainly understand the need for it given the press of business. However, we would ask that, it that is allowed, that we be given a similar extension and that we be required, then, to file our response to that by Friday, October 6th, which also accommodates my schedule, because this task will fall to me, and as the Court is aware, I will have other obligations during the week of the 25th of September. So that's the only thing I wanted to state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll then try to come back to you as soon as we possibly can, Mr. Milovancevic, with an answer on point 3. If that is all, we can call the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated, Mrs. Vujanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujanic, I remind you that at the beginning of your testimony you made a declaration to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. You are still bound by that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Vujanic?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We shall now continue our examination-in-chief, and I should like to ask you once again, just as I asked you at the beginning, for us to make a pause between question and answer and to speak as slowly as possible, and that refers to both you and myself. Thank you. When you were answering one of my earlier questions, Mrs. Vujanic, you said that the right to participate at the referendum that you organised as the chairman of the central electoral commission was vested in all citizens of age with a place of residential in the municipality where the vote was being held. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was such a provision on the right of the participation of all citizens of age, was it envisaged under the law?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the law regulating this right of participation make any distinctions between citizens, in terms of gender, religion, profession and nationality, or anything else?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that all citizens of the Krajina who had their places of residence in the municipality where the referendum was being held irrespective of their nationality, ethnicity, had the right to vote at that referendum?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether there were any violations of these provisions stipulated under the law, and also specified in the -- established in specific instances?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know of any such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now we shall revert to another topic. You mentioned that as a member of a delegation from the SAO Krajina and there were some 30 of you visiting the Presidency of Yugoslavia and Mr. Jovic, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that representatives of the Krajina, especially from Slavonia and Kordun, had used some data that you personally found astonishing. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the delegation of the SAO Krajina acquaint anybody else, apart from Mr. Jovic, with that data when you were in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the meeting with Mr. Jovic finished, the chief of the cabinet of Mr. Jovic approached us, and he told us that President Milosevic had expressed a desire for us to come and see him in the Serbian Presidency. So after this meeting, we went to the Presidency of Serbia, and were received there by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who this -- what kind of talk did you have with Mr. Milosevic on that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a talk that was completely identical -- identical to the one that we had had with Mr. Jovic, in the SFRY Presidency, simply the people actually unloaded their chests and mostly spoke about what was their major concerns, and these were people from Slavonia, Baranija, spoke about what had transpired, that people had been made redundant, laid off, like the instance which I mentioned the last time this example of a doctor from Pakrac. So we had similar examples also being presented at this meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Were there -- was there -- was there any reaction to that on that occasion by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I experienced both meetings just as a place where we could vent our grievances, and they let us just talk and say what we had. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that you were the chairman, the president of the central electoral commission and you also referred to the first multi-party elections which ended in May 1990. Who won? What parties won in Knin then?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Serbian Democratic Party, headed by Dr. Milan Babic that won the elections in Knin then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The municipal public attorney and then -- as the municipal public attorney and later the chairman of the electoral commission, did you have any dealings, any ties, any relations I mean, political ones, with Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well basically I did not engage in politics. I just did my professional work as chairman of this commission, and I was chairman of that commission because I was graduated jurist. But as the public attorney, I -- I did have such dealings. I was the public ombudsman in a way, of course, and as public attorney, I had to act in accordance with the law, meaning that I dealt to help people in the matter of property relations and property issues, and I didn't need any power of attorney from either the municipal head, or the executive council. And no contract or agreement dealing with property relation could be considered valid if it did not have the seal of the attorney, of the public attorney. So that was my role, but as regards politics, I was just a member of this delegation when I was invited, and we had several contacts along those lines, but that was it. Let me just mention. I am not -- I was not a member of any party. I was a member of the Legal Communists while it existed, but later I was not a member of any party either in Knin or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to hear from Mr. Babic, what his -- what the leadership of Serbia thought about the referendum, the referendum question and about the establishment of the government?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when these elections were being prepared, namely after the Assembly had taken this decision and nominated me, appointed me as president of the Electoral Commission, I had contacts with the late Mr. Babic. In fact, I was in his apartment with some associates of mine a couple of times and I remember quite well this text which was to be placed on the ballot. It was formulated by him personally. He said, actually -- worded his text, were we in favour of SAO Krajina's annexation to Serbia? He said that Mr. Milosevic was extremely angry with that text, and that he asked him, Babic that is, that it should not go, that the text should be whether we were for remaining with Serbia and Montenegro or with Yugoslavia. Not for this annexation. Then he told him that he could not order him what to do, and according to him, then there was this large falling out between the two of them. However, that original text was used. It was written by Mr. Babic with his own hand, and we had it printed in the printing enterprise Mladost for use at the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your reply that from 1975 to 1983 you had worked as a criminal law judge, as a law in the criminal department, and as such did you see any criminal complaints that had been processed by Mr. Martic as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see such complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your professional opinion was regarding the quality of the complaints or the lack of their quality. Of course I don't mean to suggest any opinion to you, of course. What were they like?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you this. You know probably how the procedure goes. First the criminal complaint is lodged, which is done by the SUP and its workers. And as far as I remember, at the time Mr. Martic was an inspector. So I had occasion to look at his complaints, as well as any others. And when, a later law was passed, the police complaints could be singled-out. But initially they were a part of the file, a component part of the file. They had been processed very well, and what is of the essence -- and this is something I do wish to stress because I have come here to say -- to tell the truth and only the truth, and especially as a person of the same profession -- it never happened, and there have been cases like that, namely, Mr. Martic was very consistent and very professional in doing his job and I can say that according to what I saw of his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can we say on the basis of what you said, that he acted in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you had seen criminal complaints that Mr. Martic submitted to the Prosecutor's office and to the Court from 1975 to 1983. But can you tell me, did you ever come to meet Mr. Martic and when was that, if that is the case?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipal court in Knin where I worked also conducted investigations from the competence of the municipal court until 1977 when investigation centres were set up. But until the first of July, 1977 when such investigations were formed. But he worked exclusively at orders of the judge of the Municipal Court, of the District Court. So as I liked to rather go in a police car rather than drive a car myself, and it goes without saying that the police was always there to inspect the scene, so that in these goings to inspection sites with the police, we all, of course, knew each other because Knin is a small place and generally speaking I had a very good cooperation with the Knin SUP as a criminal judge, as well as when it came to action in regard of the families of the injured, of injured parties. I had eight deaths among my cases, because of alcoholic -- driving while intoxicated and I had different cases. I had very good cooperation with the SUP in Knin. I would always cooperate in a very timely manner. Also when it came to securing people that needed security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I to take it that you actually came to know the accused quite well?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You talked about the referendum which was held in 1991. In 1991 there was a whole series of other events that happened. Can you tell us, do you have any experiences or any information regarding the conduct of Mr. Martic in that particular behaviour, specifically in terms of his relationship towards the citizens? Did he make any distinctions between the citizens, that is the essence of my question.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was born in 1937 and was a refugee myself, after the Second World War and when the first refugees reached Kijtanje from the Zadar hinterland and when I heard that on Radio Knin, I took it very hard. And I went there on my own as a citizen, on my own initiative and I saw a multitude of refugees in an abandoned school, which was without any electricity, there was no water. It was completely empty. It hadn't worked for some five or six years. So I took this very hard and I couldn't sleep all night thinking how I could help those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, can I interrupt you. Are you talking about the abandoned school building in Kistanje and about the refugees? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So you said you went to that school after hearing that there was some refugees there and you indeed found them there?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you were telling us what you planned to do in that situation. Can you tell us, first, where the refugees were from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I just get contextualised in terms of time here. These are refugees at Kistanje and from the Zadar hinterland, you have talked about -- you are talking about them in relation to the Second World War. Is that when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's when you were hit hard and you didn't know how you could help them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. [Interpretation] No. Those were refugees that was in the period in the summer of 1998. I remember that because I remember how people were dressed. I think they were from Ravni Kotori, the area behind Zadar, from Zadra hinterland. And those people were refugeed and temporarily housed in that school building in Kistanje, which fell into disuse after the new school was built. But it was by all means in the summer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear you. How are they connected with the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I was saying that I, as a child, was a refugee in World War II, and that's what moved me to go there when I heard over Radio Knin that refugees had come in. That brought back memories from my childhood and that moved me to go there and see with my own eyes what was going on with those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clears the point. You hadn't said so initially. So can I ask, when you are asked a question, try to confine yourself to the question that is asked. I'm sure as a judge you understand the need for precision, because now you confused us. Of course you didn't say "I was myself a refugee after the world war, Second World War." So it seemed to me like you were saying these were people from, who were refugees from the Second World War. So please try to confine yourself to exactly what is being asked and answer just that question. You are on your feet, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just wonder if we could just ask one more time about the date of this event, because the date -- it sort of stands out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just wonder if it is correctly translated or if there was a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now you're saying these people who were in this school in Kistanje, what year was this? And what month and date was it when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was year 1991. I can't remember the date, of course, but it was in summer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's it. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujanic, can you tell us very briefly who were those people? How were they dressed and did they need help? How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that there were people from Ravni Kotori, that's the hinterland of Zadar, mainly from villages. As they told us themselves they had been on their farms that very morning. And later that day they found themselves in this abandoned school building, children, elderly people. They just had little knapsacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say they ran away from their farms that morning. They ran away from whom, from what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, it may be a question of interpretation. I didn't hear the witness say they ran away from their farms. She says as they told us themselves, they had been on their farms that very morning, and later that day they found themselves in this abandoned school. I was still waiting to hear how they found themselves getting there. How did they get away from the farm to the school. Sorry, yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. I feel a little compelled to object, because there is nothing about this on the 65 ter summary. It's the first time we are learning about -- that there was going to be testimony about this event and it is obviously this -- obviously not a surprise to Mr. Milovancevic, because he has elicited it and seems to know what she is talking about, and I would object to evidence on this point since it's not been put on -- we received no notice of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend from the Prosecution is right as far as the objection is concerned, he's right in saying we had not announced it. But the fact is, I'm surprised myself by the witness's answer, and since she already mentioned it I'm trying to avoid further confusion by clarifying it. With your leave, I would like to finish with this one question and will not delve into this topic any further. But in the proofing, we did not deal with this topic at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't deal with it Mr. Milovancevic and you are surprised by it. You are not going to ask questions about it simply because I asked questions about it. I asked questions about it because I didn't understand what was happening. I am trying to relate this whole story to the rest of the witness's evidence, and I just didn't see where it comes from and how it comes in. Now, if indeed it is objectionable on the basis that it had not been notified in your 65 ter notice, it looks to me like there is no need for you to ask any further questions about it. Maybe we should abandon it and get to the next point, Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujanic, in the course of 1991, do you know, what was the attitude of Mr. Martic towards Croat citizens? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry because of this misunderstanding. It was sort of introduction into what I am about to say. This point that I was trying to make that I was involved in humanitarian work and it was precisely then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, can I interrupt you. We have ruled that piece of evidence out of order. Forget about it. Answer the question: Do you know anything about Mr. Martic's attitude towards Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. I had a jury person, Mrs. Katica Cacic, for a long time. She was otherwise teacher of geography and I knew her from before, because she was a tenant in the same building where I lived. One day she came to my door in tears and I knew her well, as well as her husband. And her husband at that time had a surgery in Split. So seeing her in tears, I asked what was going on, and she told me that some people barged into her apartment. What people? Some refugees. And I told her, why don't you stay at my place? We'll deal with it somehow. She told me that she was going to her relatives instead, but I really went to see the then Minister of Justice, Mr. Markovic, the next morning, and I also called Mr. Martic, who was secretary of the SUP at the time, or chief or whatever, and told him what had happened. We agreed of course that these things were completely out of order. On the same day, the people who who haved into the apartment of Branko Cacic were made to move out, were evacuated, on the orders of Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mrs. Vujanic, for interrupting you. Can you please specify the time period for this incident involving your jury person.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what I said just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Katica Cacic?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1991, just at the time when those refugees arrived from the Zadar region. It was the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please. You wanted to tell us about another incident when I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When refugees arrived from Drnis -- and that's what I meant with my introduction about being involved in humanitarian work together with my friends -- there were lots of Serbs and Croats among the refugees. And I remember well that evening, maybe about 9 o'clock, even ten o'clock, it happened in the trade union hall where we did this humanitarian work, Mr. Martic came and told me, personally, because I was the leader of that group of friends, and he told me: There are some Croats among the refugees who just came. Please, don't let anything happen. Receive them as well as you receive the others. That's what Mr. Martic told me, personally. And indeed there were Croats in that group. I remember a couple of people whom I recognised, parents of a famous basketball player, and I remember that woman was very tall and we couldn't find any clothes of the proper size for her, so I brought some from my own home. And I will remember that forever; that is something that I know for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you. I'm sorry. I'm concerned about time, Mrs. Vujanic. Can I just ask you one point. What was the ethnicity of your jury person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. You can move on, Mr. Milovancevic. Please control the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujanic, a moment ago you mentioned refugees, both Serbs and Croats who were flowing in from the area of Drnis, correct?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was going on in Drnis to make those refugees flee, and when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that I did that humanitarian work in the summer and autumn 1991. The army conducted some sort of operations there. That's not something I know a lot about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say the army was conducting operations, which army do you mean?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were these people running away from the operations of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I know is that they arrived in Knin and we received them as refugees. To tell you the truth, what they ran away from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That last point is the answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujanic, did you follow the trial of Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of it. As far as I could manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about his plea bargain?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to object again. This is also not on the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw this question, Your Honour. I have no further questions in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujanic. My name is Alex Whiting, I'm one of the Prosecutors in this case. And I am going to ask you a few questions. You testified on Friday about the death of Vaso Pecar, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified that you thought it occurred at the end of 1990. In fact, it occurred in the spring of 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I really can't remember the dates. I can remember some dates that are associated in my mind with very particular, very special cases, but that's something that doesn't happen often.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So just bringing it back to this event, the death of Vaso Pecar, are you saying that you don't remember the date of when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's not known who killed Vaso Pecar, is it?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know only what was being said and what I heard then, that Ustashas had killed him. I can tell you the version that circulated in Knin and that you could hear at his funeral --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well madam ---

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that his --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- grandfather had died the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, you never heard a particular or specific person identified as the killer of Vaso Pecar, did you, in those stories that circulated around Knin?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you explain for me, then, how it is that there would be stories saying that Ustashas killed him, stories which you repeated in your direct evidence and just repeated a few moments ago? That is, if the killer was not known, how is it known that -- how can it be said that Ustashas killed him?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably the way he was killed and the place where he was found that indicated that. I can only tell you what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, Mrs. Vujanic, you know that Ustashas are -- that's a reference to people in a government from the Second World War, right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you refer to somebody as an Ustasha, that is a very kind of extremist thing -- I mean that is a very extreme statement to say about somebody, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably in that period, when it all started in our region, the words "Ustashas" and "Chetniks" were very frequently used on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Not just in that period, also last Friday in your evidence, right? You told this Trial Chamber on Friday that Ustashas had killed him. It's at page 64 of your evidence on Friday.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I heard. That's all I can tell you, what people were saying at his funeral ceremony attended by several thousand people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You would agree with me that it's impossible, from the way he was killed and the place he was found, to conclude that Ustashas had killed him, right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can only tell you again, I did not conduct that investigation to be able to tell you what was established and how. I'm just telling you what was being said by everybody that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But madam, madam --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By his neighbours that Ustashas had killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, this is the year 2006. You're testifying in front of the Tribunal in The Hague. Did you believe, on Friday, that this kind of information was reliable enough for you to share with the Judges and to testify to? Was that your belief?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand, was what my belief?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you're telling us, well this is just what I heard, and so forth. But my point is that you, you felt this, I take it you felt this important enough and reliable enough to share it in your testimony on Friday with the Trial Chamber. Is that the case? Did you find it reliable and important to share that information?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reiterate that I'm only saying to you what was being said in Knin at the time when he was killed and people were very upset about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, madam --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the perpetrator was never found.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, madam, that that term "Ustasha" was a frightening term for Serbs in 1991, and even today?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll share with you my personal opinion and also what you could hear people tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just answer the question. If you could please just answer the question. Would you agree with me that the term "Ustasha" was a frightening term, caused fear among Serbs in 1991? That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the word "Ustasha" is terribly upsetting to Serbs. And we all know how Mr. Glavas presented his fighters, it was on TV together with all the songs and iconography, that's the way they introduced themselves. It is nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's take this one step at a time. You've told us now that the term Ustasha is terribly upsetting to the Serbs. Would you agree with me also that you have used that term rather loosely in your testimony. That is you you refer to somebody as an Ustasha who is not even -- has never even been identified. So would you agree with me that you use that term rather loosely?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We obviously didn't understand each other. I only said what happened after the death of Vaso Pecar, what happened in Knin, what people were saying, that's all I said. I am not the one who pointed the finger at anybody or called them Ustashas. That's probably the difference between your question and my answer. I'm just telling you what people were saying at the time he was killed by Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you believe that?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you believe that to be true? Did you think he had been killed by Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, yes. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Based on what?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed in his own village, which faces Kijevo and I don't know who else could have killed him, especially if you take into account the fact that his grandfather, too, met his death in the same way in World War II. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, is it fair to say that you thought that all members of the HDZ or all members of the Croatian police were Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, how is it that you conclude that the person who killed Vaso Pecar is an Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, the witness used a plural. She spoke of the Ustashas killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry. The people who killed him. Well let me ask you this. Do you know if he was killed by more than one person? Or was he killed by one person? Or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me go back to something that you said earlier, which is that, you made a reference to Mr. Glavas. We've heard his name before in this trial, and he, Mr. Glavas, you would agree with me is an extremist, was considered then and now an extremist in Croatia, right, and within the HDZ? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now possibly yes, but for a long time he was the -- he was the flag bearer of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you mean --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my own personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you base that, on what, that conclusion that he was the flag bearer?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I base that conclusion on the fact that proceedings that are now being instituted against him, although I live in Belgrade I have cable television and I watch Croatian TV every day and I follow the developments. And it is obvious that there is some kind of will now to finally bring him to justice, whether it will succeed or not is another matter, but it's obvious that he is no longer in HDZ what he used to be. It's a matter of some internal conflicts into which I don't want to go. But it's obvious that he is not -- he doesn't have the same role in the HDZ now that he used to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But that doesn't answer the question of how it is that you concluded that he was the flag bearer back in 1991.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on his public appearances that I saw with my own eyes on television, I heard him say to his fighters, he salutes them with God bless you Ustashas, salute Ustashas, what are you afraid of. Those were films that I saw on TV, I mean documentary footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. And we have that clip in evidence here. The truth is, Mrs. Vujanic, isn't it, that Mr. Glavas did not represent the majority of people in the HDZ or in Croatia, did he? He was an extremist on the fringe, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I know. I was never particularly interested or involved in politics. I told you what I know from what I follow of politics. Unfortunately, that's the way things are. I did not count these men. All I can tell you is that with the rise of the HDZ, things started going downhill in our region.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, on the topic of Ustashas, you testified that you got to know Milan Martic quite well. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he use the term "Ustashas"?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My contacts with Mr. Martic were indeed official ones, when I worked as a judge, then in my other capacity, which I described here, so he never used that term, neither did I. I just related to you what the people were saying after the death of Vaso Pecar, and please see it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why didn't you use the term Ustashas? What was the reason for not using it?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not use either the term Ustashas or the term Chetniks. Maybe in some talks they could have been used, but I never felt the need to use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness hasn't actually answered the question and told you why or why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, if you would answer the question, please. Why didn't you use that term? What was wrong with it?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I come from -- I hail from different parts. I came to Knin, and I came from a different area. This term, the Ustashas, is something that I came to understand as it were and here. In Knin, that was not something which was familiar, as familiar to me as it was to the people who lived in these areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So why did you take the decision not to use the term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not a matter of any decision. I didn't give it any thought, in fact. I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I thought you had said earlier that it was not a word which you used. And what the Trial Chamber wants to know is, why you avoided the use of the word. Let me help you. Would you consider it a pejorative or derogatory term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you frankly, as I said a while ago, I grew up in a different area where this was not as used as it was in these parts. I may have used it in some talks, but I never used it in a political sense, making any statements or such. But I do have to say that in that particular time, that was used in those areas as an association to the Second World War, and this was a much discussed topic, the resurgence of that, what the Ustashas had done in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am, what is remarkable about your testimony is that you are so clear in your mind that you never used the term, and in fact you have been so observant of this term that you are testifying today that you know for a fact that Mr. Martic has never used that term, but you are not able to tell us why. Obviously this term has occupied your mind intensively, that you have been able to make a mental note of who uses it and who doesn't, and that you yourself don't use it. You've got to be able to tell us why you don't -- you didn't use the term.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean officially or privately? And I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You haven't told us whether you have not used it officially or privately. You have just said you have not used it. Why didn't you use it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply did not use it because it was just not part of my usage. I was not from those parts, and up to the 1990s I had not practically heard it said. Of course, unless I was reading some -- reading matter referring to the Second World War, but where I came from it was not mentioned in those times. It started to be mentioned often in the 1990s when these hapless events started to transpire there, and that's just -- so I was just minding my professional business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is my observation, precisely that. Why have you not used it since you came across it in the 1990s? And you have found it so easy to use it in Court in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge and Your Honours, please understand this. When I was talking about the case of Vaso Pecar, I only repeated what the people in Knin were saying. I never said that that was what I knew, that he had been killed by the Ustasha. I just related what the people had been saying at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's go back to your answer. Why did you take the decision not to use that term, since you came to know of it? And how do you come to -- let's put that aside. Why did you decide not to use the term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly speaking, I cannot guarantee you that I never used it. I may have used it at times, so that I cannot recall. But simply there was no particular need for me to either use the term the Chetniks or the Ustashas. I was in a quite different field, doing my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have you ever used the word Chetnik? Have you ever used the word Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Probably. Especially since in the area where I was born there had been Chetniks. The Italians were there and the Chetniks were there so that I may have used it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Since 1990 when you were in Knin, have you ever used the word Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I frankly cannot remember, just as in the case of the Ustashas. It is quite possible I may have used it, perhaps then again I didn't use these terms, but I don't consider it to be that important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the Chamber to accept as your testimony? You say you never used the words, but you may probably have used them, but it was not in you so you never used them. What is the fact here and what is fiction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I allow the possibility that I may have used the term Ustashas and Chetniks as well, but I cannot assert with certainty that either was the case, because I really never paid any particular attention to that, but I do allow the possibility that I have used both terms on occasion in some talks. I couldn't swear that I haven't used them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's focus again on Mr. Martic, and if we could see Exhibit 213, please, in evidence. Madam, I'm going to show you a newspaper article that's in evidence. It is from the 7th of July, 1991, and it's published in the newspaper Tanjug, which you know is a newspaper that was published in Belgrade; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Isn't this a press agency, Tanjug?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I'm sorry. And it's based in Belgrade, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I'm actually not sure if this is a press release, what exactly the status of this is. Thank you, Your Honour. If we could go to the second page of the B/C/S and to the bottom of the English page, please. You just have to blow up the last two paragraphs. It says: "Martic pointed at the current Croatian authorities as their common enemy, describing them as an Ustasha state, which does not wish well either to us or the Yugoslav Army." Do you remember Mr. Martic referring to the Croatian government or Croatia as an Ustasha state, in July of 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall such things. I do not claim that he hasn't said that. I came here to testify about what I personally know, from the fields that I covered. I do not recall this particular article.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, were you --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But what I said was, in talking to me, he never used such a term.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, were you -- you had gotten to know Milan Martic quite well. Were you familiar with his public statements that he was making at the time?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember quite well in respect of Milan Martic when the people were protesting against the weapons being seized from the arms, when he was talking on their behalf. But more than 15 years have passed and now who said what and for what particular newspaper, I couldn't possibly remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, madam -- I'm sorry, ma'am, but you have just been telling us now when you were led by Defence counsel, that you knew Mr. Martic well, and he used to make complaints, he was working very well. And actually, I have a question that I am going to ask you here later, about that issue. You know, you can't now turnaround and tell us that all you know is, what did you say, all you know about Mr. Martic is when people were protesting against weapons. You didn't even mention weapons when you were being led. You mentioned him working with you and his people very smoothly, and you were asked, you came to know Mr. Martic very well, and you said "yes." Do you remember that question by Defence counsel? Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, once again I ask, which is fact here, Do you know Mr. Martic very well? Or all you know is what he said about, only concerning the protest against weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that I did know Mr. Martic and I did know him when I was a judge and I adhere to that statement. I knew Mr. Martic in this period, yes. I know him, not as I know many people from Knin, because Knin is a small place and I know many people from Knin, but I know him also along the lines of professional cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to round off your point? Or you want to round it off when you come back?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we can take the break. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. We will take the break and come back at 4 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this to you, Mr. Whiting, but can we just deal with the question that was raised by -- oh, please be seated, ma'am. Sorry. The question that was raised by Mr. Milovancevic that he would like us to apply our minds to, and then we can move on. Mr. Milovancevic, the Chamber has found itself inclined to grant you the extension. Now, can we just get clarity. You want an extension to what date? The 25th you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, until this next -- first next Monday. The deadline was this Thursday, and we meant to ask for an extension until the next Monday, which is seven days from this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you realise that next Monday you will not be here? But your office will attend to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do realise, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting, on that basis, you want an extension up to the 6th of October? Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it's granted. Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic up to the 25th. Mr. Whiting up to the 6th. Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, so just before the break, I understood you to testify that you knew Mr. Martic well when you were a judge, which was up until 1983. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's fair to say, is it not, that during 1990, during 1990 and 1991, you either did not follow his public statements or you are unable to remember them now, with the exception of one statement that you referred to in your testimony about when weapons were seized. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot remember almost, actually not almost, but 15 years have passed. I probably have read some of those statements, but I cannot recall them. I do recall what transpired in contact with me, and that is what I have told this Court already. And as regards any other statements, I cannot say anything about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, would you not, that in 1991 you couldn't, in July of 1991, you couldn't describe all of the authorities of Croatia or the Croatian state as an Ustasha state, could you? You couldn't apply that term "Ustasha" to the entire Croatian state or all of the Croatian authorities, could you?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot characterise as such the entire Croatian people where I also have and had relatives, among who I had and have kin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, I'm going to interrupt you because I wasn't asking about the entire Croatian people. I was talking about the Croatian state, or Croatian authorities. You couldn't describe the Croatian state or the Croatian authorities as an Ustasha state, could you?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a very complex question, but it is a fact that we regarded those authorities, including me personally, as such. Now, for me to distinguish between what comprises the Croatian authorities and the Croatian state, that would require some time for explanation and a number of approaches to the issue, but it is a fact that regreably that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, madam, when I asked you earlier if you thought all members of the Croatian MUP or all members of the HDZ were Ustashas, you said "no."

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, of course not. I have no such information to be able to state that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, it's fair to say that you couldn't -- you also cannot say that all of the Croatian authorities are Ustashas; could you?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course I couldn't, I cannot. I can only state my opinion, but of course I couldn't say something definite on that score. I would have to have some judgement or some finding, but in this way it is something which is quite undefined.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, not only is it undefined, it is also untrue, isn't it? Not all the Croatian authorities were Ustashas, were they? And you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably not all of them were. I can speak about those I had dealings with within my department, the judiciary, I mean from that aspect, but I was not in politics, so I can only relate what it was that we all felt. But as for such a definition, I have no right to give such a charaterisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will move on from this topic. You testified about the new Croatian constitution of December 1990. You remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever actually read the constitution, yourself?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So then you are aware that the constitution guaranteed Serbs equality with Croats and guaranteed them all ethnic rights, right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot recall the details of that constitution. I have read it, of course, but what was disasterous about that constitution was the fact that the Serbian people, who had been --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, I'm going to interrupt you because I want to focus on my question now. Do you recall -- you say you can't recall the details. Do you recall this detail that the constitution guaranteed Serbs equality with Croats and guaranteed them all ethnic rights?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall that. I cannot remember the text of the constitution. It would be elusory for me to try to recall the text of the constitution after 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: About you you do remember, after 15 years, that the status of the Serbs changed in the constitution. That you do remember, right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I personally feel the consequences, and even after 15 years I feel the consequences of that particular thing, because I cannot return to my flat, to my house, and I remember that because of that, because that affected, afflicted the most, me personally and my people generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that you -- as I recall it, you said that you left Knin in 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 1st of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was your decision, correct?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the constitution, even though the constitution was adopted in December of 1990, nothing happened to you and your flat or your house in 1991, 1992. And in 1992 you decided, on your own, to leave Knin, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- yes, I came -- I went to Belgrade from Knin on another private business, and after several days, I decided to stay on in Belgrade with my family, a part of my family however remaining in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And have you lived in Belgrade since 1992 to the present?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now when you say you don't recall that the constitution of December of 1990 guaranteed Serbs equality with Croats and guaranteed them all ethnic rights, are you saying that, that this is -- that you just really don't remember either way? Or is this the first time you've heard that? Or does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. Would you be so kind as to repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say you don't recall that the constitution of December 1990 guaranteed Serbs equality with Croats and their ethnic -- all their ethnic rights, are you saying you don't remember that either way, or are you saying that you don't think that was the case? Or just, if you could explain a little more what you're saying about that.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a while ago that I read that constitution at that time, and even when, with laws that I use in my work, I always have to consult the relevant article. I cannot recall it by heart. But what I do know is what the consequence of that constitution is throughout the area, namely today, I myself, my family, and my friends and acquaintances who want to return to their flats, are unable to do so. We try to return to the village house belonging to my husband, which is entirely devastated, if not torn down altogether. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- have different requirements placed before us for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, those things that you're testifying about that you say are the case now, that -- those are not a result of the constitution, are they? Those are a result of events that happened years later, in 1995 and after that, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in my view, it's these things actually started from that constitution. And with that constitution, it was the forerunner of what was to follow. Of course, I am again stating my own opinion and speaking from my own personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's move to the core of your testimony, which was about the referendum in May of 1991. I want to go back in time just a bit to the clash that occurred at Plitvice on the 31st of March, 1991. That clash occurred when the SAO Krajina police, Mr. Martic actually, sent a unit of policemen to Plitvice, including -- which included police from the special unit in Knin; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not answer questions dealing with such detail. All I know, it was a conflict between the Krajina police and Croatia's policemen. I only knew as much as I could hear, or read. I was not a direct participant and I'm not aware of details. I knew only as much as every citizen of Knin or Krajina could know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you do know, though, that there was an immediate reaction in the Krajina after that occurred, and that on the 1st of April 1991, Milan Babic issued a number of decisions, right? Were you aware of that? Or is that something you don't know about?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I remember is a decision of Milan Babic's from August, when he declared a state of war, but I really can't remember all of the individual decisions. It's probable that we all read them and heard about them, but I can't remember anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can refresh your recollection. If we could look at Exhibit 144, please. And if we could just blow up the top half there, yes. Do you see, madam, this is a decision dated the 1st of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do we have the English version at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't know it was not up. We should have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's issued by Milan Babic, president of the Executive Council of the SAO Krajina. And it is a decision to join the SAO Krajina to the Republic of Serbia which is in the very first article. Do you remember this occurring on the 1st of April, 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This is actually the first time I'm seeing the text of the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, even though it's the first time you're seeing the text of the decision, did you hear about this decision at the time?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this particular decision. I don't know if I heard about it. All I know is that there was this decision about the referendum that I was familiar with at the time when I was chairman of that committee, but I don't remember this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you were -- madam --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you were familiar with the decision on the referendum; that's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look at that, please. That is Exhibit 148. And if we could look at the very top paragraph. I'm going to wait until we get the English. Do you see that in the very first paragraph of this decision, which you say you are familiar with, it makes reference to the decision that we were just looking at from the 1st of April, 1991. Based on the right of people to self-determination, the previously-adopted decision on the asession of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina to the Republic of Serbia, taken by the Executive Council of the SAO Krajina at its session of 1 April, 1991. So now, -- now that you see that, do you think that maybe you knew about --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified earlier today, when you were asked questions by Defence counsel, that -- so this, just to be clear, this is on the 30th of April, 1991, and the previous document was on the 1st of April, 1991. You testified that when Milan Babic -- when Milan Babic wanted the referendum to be about annexing the SAO Krajina to Serbia, that Slobodan Milosevic got angry and wanted it to be about Yugoslavia. Right? Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact, Milan Babic wanted the referendum to be -- have the same wording as the decision of 1 April 1991 and to say -- to ask whether the voters were in favour of annexing the SAO Krajina to Serbia, right; that it would follow that same wording.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this 30th of April, 1991, I don't know how the decision was formulated. I was not -- I was not a direct participant in that. But if you're interested in the part that I knew about as chairman of the committee, when we were about to formulate the contents, the text of the ballot, Milan Babic said, in a circle of his associates, that Milosevic was very much against that formulation being placed on the ballot, including the words accession of Krajina to Serbia; that he wanted the text to read: Do you want the Krajina to remain within the same state as Serbia and Montenegro? And if you want to ask me things about the part of the work in which I was directly involved as chairman of that committee, I can answer that question positively.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And -- well, we'll get to that topic, but I want to see if you know anything about these things since you testified about these matters. In fact, Milan Babic changed -- changed the question as a result of pressure from Slobodan Milosevic. He changed it from simply asking whether the voters wanted the SAO Krajina to be annexed or become part of Serbia, and he included becoming part of Yugoslavia and that's how the question is phrased here in this decision, right? He added the part about staying in Yugoslavia. Right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was a result of the pressure from Slobodan Milosevic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I heard from late Milan Babic, namely that Slobodan Milosevic was terribly angry that those were the words he used, about the idea to put this wording in the ballot. I can only tell you about what he passed on to us. He wanted the referendum to be about whether Krajina wanted to remain within Yugoslavia together with Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, this is the text that was actually used in the ballot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, madam, Slobodan Milosevic wanted it to speak about Yugoslavia, because the strategy of the Serb leaders in Belgrade and in particular of Slobodan Milosevic was, at that time, to speak about preserving Yugoslavia rather than about creating a Serb state. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, the entire Serb people in Krajina, that is in Croatia, was in favour of preserving Yugoslavia, and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With Slovenia moving towards the cesession and Croatia moving towards cessesion, preserving Yugoslavia was becoming -- was, in essence, no different than preserving the Serb areas in Yugoslavia, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yugoslavia was a state where we all lived very well, regardless of our ethnicity and the particular area where we lived. And it's a fact, again, that the Serb people were scattered across many regions, including Croatia and it was in their vital interest to preserve Yugoslavia. And it's certain that these people really wanted that. From what I know, and from what we understood, the Belgrade leadership also wanted and worked for the preservation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But for them, the preservation of Yugoslavia meant keeping together the Serb areas, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we wanted the entire Croatia to remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Serb people could have stayed within that Croatia as a part of Yugoslavia. Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So ma'am?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it didn't happen that way and that's how it came about that Krajina separated itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So Madam, you're not aware that by say June or July of 1991, Slobodan Milosevic didn't care if Slovenia left Yugoslavia and if the Croatian, majority parts of Croatia left Yugoslavia so long as the Serb part of Croatia stayed in Yugoslavia? You're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you frankly I'm not a politician. I was not so involved in those things. I know just as much as the regular citizen knew. But what I know, that it's the dissolution of Yugoslavia that finally brought about this situation that we have today, that many people do not have any homes to return to. And what I told you here is what I knew about the referendum I was involved in and what I heard from Mr. Babic about his talks with Mr. Milosevic. As for the other things, I cannot tell you with any certainty, because I'm not a politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, okay --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and it was not my intention to speak about the things I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's, let's continue talking about the referendum. You testified on Friday that the turnout in the referendum was 100 per cent. Do you remember that testimony? It's at page 73 of the testimony from Friday.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really say how many people turned out, but I seem to remember a percentage of 98 point something per cent. In fact 98.8 per cent voted for, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know that the turnout was large. I don't know how many, but out of those who turned out, I know that 98 point something per cent voted for. I cannot give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you appreciate the difference between telling us how many -- what percentage of people voted for, and what percentage of people turned out to vote? Those are two very different things, correct?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified on Friday, and we spoke earlier today about being precise in testimony. You testified on Friday that the turnout was 100 per cent. Are you changing that testimony today?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that out of the number that turned out, over 98 per cent voted for, that is still etched in my memory. But I don't remember how many turned out. I think -- this is very viable, the material has been sealed, all of it, and it's been filed, archived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well madam --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents are available for verification. We can easily find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well I'm just reading from your testimony on Friday when you said -- it's at my page 73. It's probably around 8472, the page numbers shifted a little bit. But you said: "The referendum was conducted in all the municipalities which I enumerated. The turnout was 100 per cent shall I say." That was your testimony on Friday?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly it was a clumsy interpretation. All I know is that 98 per cent or more voted for. I don't know. Maybe I expressed myself clumsily, or -- anyway, what I'm telling you now is that a very large percentage turned out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Like --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And 98 per cent or more voted for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyway, it's all on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is. Let's look at your report, 149, which is Exhibit 149, which is in evidence. And if we could look at page 6 of the B/C/S and page 4 of the English, please. I think we have the B/C/S on the English screen. Now, do you see in the last sentence of the document that it says that 79.48 per cent of the voters on the electoral roll came out to vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Whiting. We still don't have the English one. I have B/C/S on both screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have English on mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you? Okay. Let me try again. It has now come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's the last sentence at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you accept now that the turnout was in fact 79.48 per cent? Right? Do you see that at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I stand by this. It is certain, what is written in the record is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was verified by all the members of the commission of which I was the chairperson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, we just need to try to save time here, so you fully answered the question when you said "yes." Now, I would like to look specifically at the turnout in the Knin municipality, and if we could look at page 3 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S. You have it on the English, but now you have lost it. Now you have the B/C/S on the English. Thank you. We're focusing on section 10, the Knin municipality. Do you see that it says the number of registered voters was 40,520, and the number of people who voted was 37,141, or 91.66 per cent. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And 91.66 per cent is almost identical to the percentage of Serbs that were living in the Knin municipality at that time, according to you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
