utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I know the figure was about 92 per cent of Serbs, but I cannot give you the exact figure. I can only say that I stand by this record, that's what the original committee wrote --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and recorded and I don't want to comment further on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, I didn't ask you anything about standing by the record. I was only asking if the percentage of voters in the Knin municipality matched almost identically the percentage of Serbs in the Knin municipality and I take it your answer is "yes."

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, almost. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, by the way, you testified that -- you testified that the -- a number of people came from Zadar and other places outside the SAO Krajina to vote, and that under the Rules, they were not allowed to vote because they didn't have residence in the SAO Krajina, right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why didn't you just tell them that, tell them they were not allowed to vote and send them home?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let us get one thing straight. The people that you are referring to are not included in this number here. They were not sent away, simply because -- because we tried to avoid incidents at the polling places, if we had tried to send them away. And we talked about it within the committee. It was not according to the law to let them vote and it was out of the question, but if somebody had come such a long way from Zadar or Sibenik, we didn't want to embarass them or cause them any unpleasantness at the polling places. They were simply given a piece of paper to circle the name, but that did not have any influence on the legal procedure of the referendum, nor were their votes reflected in the vote count.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, did you tell the people who were voting, or thought they were voting, that in fact their votes would not count?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether we explained it to them, but it's a fact that their votes were not taken into account and we make that clear in the report made later to the Assembly. It's no secret. On an individual basis, we did tell some of them, not everybody, but that didn't cause any problem, nor did it detract from the legal procedure of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, this report you presented to the Assembly of the SAO Krajina, correct?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you remember Milan Babic making a speech after the report was presented?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would like to listen to part of that speech, please, and we're going to play it on the Sanction, and the English text will go alongside of it. So if we could switch over to the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "The desire and will of the Serbian people in SAO Krajina not to live in any kind of --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. Is it possible, because, to listen to the -- without it being read? Or do the interpreters have to read it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Normally for the French, it is necessary to have an English audio.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It would be nice to listen to it -- maybe if we could listen to it one time so we can hear the voice, and then we can play it again if the French booth requires it. I don't know if the French booth could give an indication. Of course I can't hear because I don't have the French microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It needs to be added into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We could do that. We could do that later. So if we can just play it and hear the voice and then read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we bring up on the e-court the transcript of that. It's ETT000-1182 because I want to look at just a few particular sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But Madam, while that that is being done, do you remember Milan Babic speaking those words at the Assembly session, after the report was submitted?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, after 15 years, I do not recall the exact words uttered by him. I do remember that after the report Milan Babic delivered a speech, but this is certainly his voice. This is an authentic recording, that much I can say, knowing his voice. But hadn't you played this, I wouldn't be able to remember. I only know that he did deliver a speech, but I cannot recall his very words after 15 years, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't expect you to remember his very words, but we're going to look at some particular sentences and see if you remember some of the meaning of some of the things he said. Now, on this, we only have the English transcript. We don't have a transcript in B/C/S, but the witness has heard it. Well, I think I -- I can ask you the first question. Do you recall him saying, just now, in the first sentence of that little clip, that the referendum showed, demonstrated that Serbs in Croatia did not want to live in any kind of Croatian state, and that was a view shared by many Serbs in the Krajina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot repeat verbatim what the late Dr. Milan Babic said, but it is a fact that having been expunged from the constitution as a constituent people, the Serbs did not want to continue living in a separate state of Croatia, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He also said, in that little clip, that the SAO Krajina belongs ethnically and historically with Serbia. And that was also a view that was shared by many Serbs in the Krajina, wasn't it, by Serb leaders in the Krajina? Not just Milan Babic, but the other Serb leaders?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia is the parent country of the Serbs irrespective of where they lived. So this is only a normal relationship towards one's parent state and especially in view of the circumstances, the dissolution of a joint state in which we all had lived phenomenal lives, whereas all of a sudden a constitution is being adopted from which you are chucked out as a constituent people, so that it is quite normal that you should -- that should only foster your basic feelings towards your parent state.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would just like to add that in the initial sentence of the transcript that we heard there is the adjective, a separate state of Croatia which is not in the English that we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm grateful to the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact Milan Babic in that passage talked about the communist period, that is the period from World War II until essentially until 1990 as a period when -- that had divided and separated the Serbs and he talked about uniting with Serbia to "correct the historical injustice that was being made to them during the period of Communism." Wasn't that the view of many Serb leaders in the Krajina at the time?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot -- I wouldn't like to comment and I'm not qualified to comment on anyone's statements. I gave you an answer loud and clear to the part to which I can give you an answer, but I did not involve myself with this subject matter. So what I can say is that the -- when this Christmas constitution was adopted, when the Serbs were expunged from it, in the way I described, this is where the story ends for me. I am no historian. I cannot comment on this portion of the statement. I do apologise, but that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're just not aware of that, you're just not aware about whether Serb leaders held that view? You don't know? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the opinions of the Serb leaders about the communist regime, that is something that I never dealt with, and that is something that I certainly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, what about -- what about towards the end of that clip, he talks about the Serbs living in a single country and about "the removal of barricades represented in the republics' boundaries." And if we could look at page -- for that, if we could look at page 4 of this transcript. I'm grateful for --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would just like to say that the original says "barriers" and not "barricades". And apart from that, there are many other things which need to be corrected in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm grateful. We will endeavour to get another translation to get all of those things corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember him saying that, talking about "the removal of barriers represented in the republic's boundaries"?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Of course I don't remember. I just heard it here, now. But what is of the essence is, when we lived in Yugoslavia, we had bound areas that were administrative bound areas, which really didn't mean a thing to us. We were all living in one state called Yugoslavia. We felt it to be our state. We felt very secure and safe in it. Whether in Croatia, in Bosnia and Montenegro, the laws were federal. We all felt that this was our state. This one country, Yugoslavia, and only in it did we feel safe and secure. That is what I can say personally, that is my feeling, the feeling of my friends and my community, my people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, Madam, Milan Babic was happy to have the republican boundaries disappear and to have Serb areas unite, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well of course, he probably wished for the Serbian areas to unite and especially after what was happening, it is only logical that we Serbs wanted some sort of a guarantee, some sort of a Yugoslavia to be set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ma'am, you answered the question. You would agree with me, would you not, that Milan Babic was the highest or at least one of the highest and most important political leaders in the SAO Krajina at the time, correct? He was president of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, could this transcript be admitted into evidence, with the understanding that we will have it -- have the translation checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The transcript is admitted into evidence and may it please be given an exhibit number, and the understanding is that the translation will be checked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next exhibit number is Exhibit 955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a few questions about your trip to Serbia. You testified that you went to Belgrade to present the results of the referendum and you were not allowed to do so, and that this was Slobodan Milosevic's decision, as you understood it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Slobodan Milosevic's decision, as was transmitted to us by the then vice president, Boro Petrovic and Pavic Obradovic who were the vice president of the Assembly of Serbia. We were there for a couple of days and it was touch and go, and in the end they said that they wouldn't accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, was it communicated to you that Slobodan Milosevic made this decision because -- for essentially political reasons, because at that time, if he had accepted this annexation, it would have been the first change in the borders in the former Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one conveyed to us the reasons or the comments of Slobodan Milosevic. The only thing we were told is that we could not go inside the conference hall, and all we wanted is that the Serbian people should hear what the decision was, because the Assembly meeting was being broadcast. But we were decidely told --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ma'am, there was no secret about this referendum. Everybody in the former Yugoslavia knew about the referendum, right? And knew the results. You nodded your head "yes." But that is not recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The referendum was absolutely public, and the results were carried in the then official bulletin, Official Gazette of the SAO Krajina. And as I've already told you, there was between 100, 150 foreign and domestic journalists on that day when the referendum was being held. What was in the head of Slobodan Milosevic when he didn't -- wouldn't allow --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, if we could look at an article from Borba, from the 22nd of May, 1991. And it's ERN 0266-6814. Now, do you see, it's the -- it should be the fourth paragraph of the article, which may not be visible. There. Okay. And if we could have the English. This is an article about the Serbian parliament considering whether to discuss the requests of the Krajina Serbs, and it says in the fourth paragraph -- I don't know if it's visible on the screen to you, it says: "It is therefore perfectly logical that the opposition should wait for the socialist party of Serbia, SPS, to speak first. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the SPS was Slobodan Milosevic's party, correct?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it goes on to say, this is is he bottom of the English, it goes on to say that, in the next paragraph that: "The national opposition has believed, from the very beginning, that any changes to the borders, prior to an agreement on the future of Yugoslavia, would, in fact, mean the start of war." And that was the problem with -- that was the problem with accepting the delegation from the Krajina, wasn't it, that Serbia did not want to be the first to endorse a change in the boundaries in the former Yugoslavia. Or put another way, did not want to be seen to be the first? Is that right? Or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can only tell you that that evening we were received by both representatives of the authorities and of the opposition, and we -- the representatives of the opposition were much closer to us. It was the socialist party that was deciding, making the decision whether we would be able to enter the Assembly or not. But I'm not sure, and I wouldn't want to give you any explanation about things that I'm not sure about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Could this document be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Exhibit 956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified about a meeting that you had with Borislav Jovic and then with Slobodan Milosevic. Do you recall that testimony that was both on Friday and today?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was a televised event, that was televised, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one in the Presidency was, and the one with Milosevic was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall that Veljko Dzakula was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, because I only know the people from Knin who were with me, Mr. Nebojsa Madinic. But actually, I did not know those people. They all introduced themselves, saying from which municipality they came, but I cannot remember all their names. I know more or less the municipalities which they represented, but not their names and I don't know whether I ever saw them again, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know that Veljko Dzakula was from Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that and I believe that he came from Pakrac, but I did not have any particular contacts with him. I just remember that he came from Pakrac. And in particular I remember that because the referendum was not conducted in Pakrac, according to the law, and that was an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember him standing up at the meeting and saying that these stories that were being recounted at this meeting were in fact an exaggeration? Do you remember him saying that?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that to tell you the truth. I don't even remember what he looked like, if he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember him -- do you remember him or somebody from Western Slavonia standing up and saying that he couldn't believe that, that all of these Serbs were being threatened even though they were from areas where Serbs were the overwhelming majority? Do you remember that being said at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember my personal impression, which was that I was astonished at what the people there were saying, because we had no such experiences in Knin. So that I was literally flabbergasted at some of their stories. And I repeat, there was this story --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which a doctor told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There is really no need to repeat your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, could you make yourself clear of what meeting you are talking where Mr. Dzakula was supposedly standing up and saying that the meeting with Jovic or Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My recollection is that it is Milosevic from the testimony. It is at page 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You were just saying their meeting, and I want it to be clear for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you just said that the televised meeting was the one with Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. But I didn't mean to say that it was necessarily the televised meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I'm sorry. Perhaps we could clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. If I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. It was, just to be clear -- thank you, Your Honour. It was in the meeting with Milosevic. Do you remember Mr. Dzakula saying these things in the meeting with Milosevic? It is at page 395-396 of our transcript. Does that help you remember this?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I -- first of all, I don't know whether Mr. Dzakula was there at all. We all introduced ourselves as representing our respective municipalities. No one in fact said their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They just said I come from this or that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There is really no need to repeat that. You said you don't remember. I won't pursue it, unless Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could you maybe tell us if you remember if there was anyone arguing in this sense. You said something about having been surprised about some statements in this meeting. Can you connect this one with the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't make any statements to that effect myself. I was personally surprised, consternated, appalled at what people there said, but I don't remember, since 15 years have passed. I don't even remember whether the name Mr. Dzakula was there or not. I didn't know him. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So therefore I was asking, was there a person, no matter who was it, arguing in this sense? Was this what you now are referring to as apalling statements of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to repeat that I personally felt that way because we had nothing of the kind, of the things that they were talking about in Knin. So that I was surprised. I was really bewildered to hear the things that they were talking about, and that is about -- that is as much as I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean? I think this is now our question. When you say, I was surprised of the things which were said there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was surprised when one of these doctors related a case and he talked about it in those meetings with Mr. Jovic and with Mr. Milosevic, which is that his calling doctor was taken away from his workplace and nothing is known about him. And he also said that people were being laid off on a wide scale, because they were Serbs, and really, I was really surprised to hear such accounts. This was televised, this meeting was televised. I mean the meeting with Mr. Jovic. But there were no records being kept so that I could perhaps jog my memory. And another thing. The Serbs from Croatia asked to be received in the Presidency as some sort of a shoulder to cry on in order to air their grievances and everybody just came and told their story, without there being any conclusions really drawn or made. So that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Was there someone who took the opposite view and said that these complaints were exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well as far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my attempt to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I think it is clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified about a Katica Cacic. Am I saying her name correctly?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cacic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Cacic.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Cacic, actually, if you can pronounce it. It's a soft "c".

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In my ear we're saying the same thing, but I can appreciate that you hear something different. In any event, this person, this person received help after you went and spoke to Mr. Matkovic and Mr. Martic, correct? That's all I needed --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I talked to Mr. Matkovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and by telephone with Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about Drnis. Did you know that on the 16th of September, 1991, Drnis was attacked by the army and the SAO Krajina police together?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the specifics about these operations, who attacked whom and when, I really don't know anything about that. I know that the army mounted an operation in Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But did you know --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know that the police also participated in that operation along with the army?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know that as a result of that operation Drnis was completely destroyed?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was never in Drnis after that and I don't know whether or how -- to what extent it was destroyed. I only solely worked with refugees and dealt with refugees, and that is the only thing that I can talk about in respect of that period, and I certainly cannot talk about things that I didn't see with my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did any of the refugees tell you that the -- that Drnis had been completely destroyed and that the police and army had participated in looting in Drnis during that operation in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. People, when they come, refugees who have to leave their -- who have had to leave their homes, whatever ethnicity they may be, they're just retched and miserable and unhappy and all they want from you is to take care of them, give them some assistance and care and, I really did not venture to talk with them about any other subject. The only thing that we discussed and -- was giving them help and the only thing that we tried to do was to give them assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could just put one last question on this topic, please. Did you know that Drnis was 75 per cent Croat in its population?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure of their per centage in Drnis, that being the municipality that I never worked in. I passed through Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on occasion. I don't know what the per centage is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I think it's a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at quarter to six. Court adjourned

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. I actually have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujanic, let me ask you a few questions as a follow-up to the cross-examination. Do you remember one question as to whether and how often you used the term Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider all Croats to be Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were Ustashas war criminals, in yours eyes?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ustashas, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, don't tell the answer. The question should be: What were Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How do you perceive the independent state of Croatia? What kind of state was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I object. Objection. I take it this is a question about the independent state of Croatia in World War II, and I didn't ask any questions about World War II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which independent state of Croatia are you asking about, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The independent state of Croatia in World War II. Only that. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then there is an objection. Do you have any response to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember another question by the Prosecutor concerning the killing of Vaso Pecar?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember answering that people were saying it was the Ustashas who killed him?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How many people, to the best of your knowledge, attended the funeral of Vaso Pecar?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended the funeral myself. I cannot estimate the number, but I had the feeling that the entire Knin was there. There were many people, and I know that people from other municipalities also came, from Bosnian municipalities and Lika municipalities, three, three-and-a-half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why do you believe it was important to mention the death of Vaso Pecar?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was important because after that, there began to prevail a sort of psychosis in Knin and everywhere I went. Tensions were high and it is from that point on that the term Ustashas was used more often, because people said, other things, that his grandfather was also killed by the Ustashas in 1941, and as I said here, I don't know first hand who killed him, but that's what the people were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend from the Prosecution asked you a number of questions regarding the so-called Christmas constitution of Croatia and he asked you, among other things, whether you were aware that ethnic rights were guaranteed to the Serbs by the constitution. Do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In response to the question from the Prosecutor, you used the word catastrophically to describe the situation surrounding the adoption of that constitution. What exactly was catastrophic about it?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was my general feeling. It was shared by the people around me. But everything that went wrong in our region started with that constitution because a people that used to be a nation building constituent people until then suddenly was turned into an ethnic minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague from the Prosecution asked you if you remember the provision of that Christmas constitution of Croatia that guaranteed ethnic rights to Serbs. I want to ask you something else. What about the practice where ethnic rights actually guaranteed in practice and were you able to exercise them?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was trying to say all along. Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I wouldn't have had any special questions. Just this last point shows me that there might be a misunderstanding. You were asked about the constitution, but you answered, in a sense which was probably apparently more related to the practice, not so much to the letter of the constitution. Is that possible? Because you were then saying, that's what I was trying to say all along. Due to this statement, I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My entire testimony before this Tribunal concerning this constitution had the objective of making the point that this constitution, throughout Serbs as a constituent people, and for me that's the end of the story. We know what that resulted in, and now, 15 years later, I, as many other people, hundreds and thousands are still unable to return to my apartment there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I don't think you can say "we know what this ended in." And this is also not what I asked you. Maybe, can you give me an example where the constitutional principle of equality of the ethnic groups was only in the book, but not in practice noticeable. Just an example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot remember the exact wording in the constitution where it says that Serbs have equal rights as the Croats, but simply it's not true. Even if it is written, in practice that is not so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Give me an example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at the time when this constitution guaranteed equality for all people regardless of ethnicity, many Serbs were dismissed from their jobs, and I have specific examples, people I know, people who had come to Knin from Zadar and other places and later found jobs in the judiciary in Knin. It's just that my acquaintanceship is limited. I know the people who worked in my line of work, and many people had indeed come from other places after losing their jobs there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions from my side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, judge. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Just one. Could you please tell me in, or rather, on the 2nd of April, 1991, which laws were the applicable laws in the SAOK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the adoption of legislation of SAO Krajina in which I was involved, it was the laws of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that applied. I specifically drafted the law on the Public Attorney's Office, and some other laws of SAO Krajina. ^^^

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you referred to federal laws, but are there not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. My apologies are in order. Are there not also laws of the republic, as well as federal laws, that are applicable to a particular territory usually? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There existed republic laws along with federal ones. There existed the legislation of the Republic of Croatia, but they did not apply on the territory of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So which laws were in existence on the 2nd of April, 1991, in terms of republican law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was the federal law, if you mean the referendum --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You told us about that before. But remember I asked you to address your mind to the question of the republic. Technically, would SAOK have been part of Croatia still?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the decision was adopted, obviously it was not a part of Croatia and did not act as a part of Croatia. We were what we were. And I can say that very shortly -- I even had a clash with Mr. Milan Babic when he offered me to be the Minister of Education which I refused. I wanted to continue in my job. Anyway, we drafted very quickly legislation of our own, and I participated in the drafting of some particular laws, such as the law on the Public Attorney's Office. And we started to implement, to enforce our own legislation in the territory of Krajina very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the decision having been taken to annex the Krajina to Serbia, and that Serbian law should be applicable, did the position remain the same? Or did it change, in terms of the applicable law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I could not say whether some Serbian laws were applied. As for my area of work, I know that the law on the Public Attorney's Office was adopted very shortly and it was that law that applied and it was a high priority, because when I spoke about the moving out of people and the case of the Cacic family, I always worked for the greatest possible implementation of laws in the territory of Krajina, and that's why I advocated expeditious adoption of our own legislation and I travelled several times to Belgrade for that purpose. For instance, in the territory of Krajina we didn't have a single economic court in the territory of Krajina. And together with a colleague of mine, who was a refugee from Slunj or some other area, Mrs. Branka Sijan, since she was from Zagreb and didn't know Belgrade, anyway I spent five days with her in Belgrade because we had consultations and we were very well received by the competent person. I'm sorry if I am keeping you. I was just trying to explain, to give you a better picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And I am very grateful to you, Mrs. Vujanic. How do you pronounce your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ljubica Vujanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Something else I want to ask you, before the republic of Serbia and Krajina was established, was there any order made or decision made by way of revocation of the fact that the laws of Serbia would be the applicable law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean when it was the Republic of Serbia and Krajina, or you mean the period of SAO Krajina? When the RSK was proclaimed I was already in Belgrade. I could not tell you one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Pardon me. I was really referring to the period between the decision and then the birth of the RSK. That is what I wanted to find out from you, but you said you are not able to give it to me. I want to thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Laws were passed between the period of SAO Krajina and the RSK period. I know that some laws, including the one I worked on, was passed while I was still in Knin, very soon after the establishment of SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions, Mr. Presiding Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Vujanic, I have a few questions to ask you, too. When you went with the delegation to Belgrade to report to the Assembly of Serbia about the results of the referendum, are you able to tell us why you chose -- when I say "you", I mean the people of Krajina -- chose to go to Serbia to give the report, why not to Bosnia Herzegovina or why not to the federal SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's some other country, Serbia, and it was a matter of course, in view of the text that was on the ballot, whether somebody agreed with it or not, and we simply thought that is the right place to submit that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying Serbia was another country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a republic within Yugoslavia. But it was our mother republic state, what will you, on the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've just been asked questions by Judge Nosworthy on my right, and you said that the laws that were applicable on the 2nd of April were the federal laws.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why not the Serbian laws, if Serbia was the mother republic you wanted to identify with? Why the federal laws?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we lived in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and we wanted to stay in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And on the entire territory of Yugoslavia, federal laws applied, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem is, you know, Mrs. Vujanic, that's precisely what I don't understand. You decide to go and report to the Assembly of Serbia, not to the Assembly of Yugoslavia. And yet you want to stay within Yugoslavia. But having decided to go and report to the Assembly of Serbia, you apply the laws of Yugoslavia and not the laws of Serbia. I'm perceiving an apparent inconsistency here and I would like you to reconcile this for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will try, to the best of my ability, to clarify that. So we lived in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia under its federal legislation and it was made up of republics, of course. At the time when we were going to the Presidency, I don't remember when it became the rump Presidency, but it's a fact that already at that time, as far as the federal parliament and the rest was concerned, I don't know if it was still functioning. But in view of the text on the ballot where the question was, whether we were going to stay within the state made up of Serbia and Montenegro and join them, it was obvious Serbia was the obvious choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand Serbia was the obvious choice. What I don't understand is why it is not the obvious choice to make Serbian laws applicable. Why do we then make federal laws applicable? Why do we want to join the republic and instead of using -- applying the laws of the republic we want to join, why do we now want the laws of the federation? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer this way. I can't remember and I can't say with any certainty that we did not apply the laws of Serbia in some areas. But I know that in some areas we applied the federal law, because it applied to the whole territory of Yugoslavia. I know, however, only the laws in my line of work, and that's the law on the public prosecutor -- sorry, Republic Attorney's Office. Very soon we adopted our own, and started implementing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. But in answer to the questions from the Judge on my right, you said, clearly, that on the 2nd of April the laws applicable were federal law, not Serbian republican laws and yet you want to join Serbia. You are not saying you want to join, to -- you're not going to report to the federal Assembly. You are reporting to the republican Assembly of Serbia. But you apply federal laws. This is what I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, it was the federal law that applied to the referendum. I told you it was the law and appointment and recall of members of parliament and local government officials. It was in keeping with that law that the referendum was held. But I'm telling you, it was in view of that text of the question of the referendum, whether to join Serbia or not. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember if the federal state was still functional at the time, if it still operated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that the text dictated that you go and report to Serbia. I just don't understand why you would only choose Serbia. If you're not able to answer, that's fine. Let's move on to another small topic. You indicated that you knew Mr. Martic when you were on the bench, and he used to bring complaints. You worked professionally, and site inspections used to go on very well. You would get into the police van because you preferred not to drive your own car. You remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you ever attend a site inspection with Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said that you were a judge from 1975 to 1983. Do you remember ever interacting with Mr. -- let me finish. Do you remember ever interacting with Mr. Martic in his capacity as a member of the police in that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Not directly. I only dealt with the criminal charges filed by him. I did not need to summon him directly, because occasionally I did see the filing officers, but not him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that period, 1975 to 1983, he was in the police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You testified also about the voting where people from Zadar came who were not entitled to vote because they did not belong to the municipality of Knin, and you allowed them to vote nonetheless. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you excluded their votes later when you calculated the votes, the results.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because they were not on the electoral lists. It's just that they came and once they were on the spot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I guess you had ballot papers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, for those people, no. We did not have ballot papers. They were on that -- the names were circled on that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Wait a minute. I'm asking about the voting. People who voted, voted on the ballot list, didn't they? On the ballot paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Everybody would get a ballot paper, including these people, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. When somebody would come to the polling place, they had to produce their ID to establish their identity. Then we would find that person on the list, and only after that we would issue them with a ballot paper, and establish that the person has voted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if you then discovered that this person is not on the voting list, what did you give this person to vote on? You don't give them the ballot paper? What do you give them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, we did not give them the voting papers, slips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did you give them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their names would just be encircled on this one separate list. Allow me, Your Honour. We would have had a major problem at the polling station, had we told those people that they are unable to vote. So we had these posters at each polling station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. And that's why it is because of this major problem that you wanted to avoid that I want to understand. I'm asking you, if I came there and I wasn't on your list of voters, what did you give me? You have just given the man in front of me a ballot paper, because he's local. What would you give me? What would you give me to vote on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You would just be recorded on the voters' list, and of course the option was either "for" or "against" and seeing that we could not give them the actual voting slips, because there was a specific number printed for the people with a place of residence, so that we didn't have any to give them, they were just reflected on the list without having been given any such slips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am, ma'am, I don't understand you. Surely -- I see other people being given a ballot paper. I have come to vote. You allow me to vote because you want to avoid problems. And I demand a ballot paper. You've got to give me a ballot paper or a voting paper, sorry, whatever you call it. I don't understand when you say you circled my name. Where do you circle my name? Because I don't want my name circled, I want a piece of paper to make my cross, otherwise I'm going to leave here, having not voted, having not made my cross and I will cause a problem that you wanted to avoid. But you avoided the problem by allowing me to vote. How did I vote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, under the law the federal law, the elections, the right to vote was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. I'm going to stop you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- predicated also on the place of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there. I'm not asking you about the law. I am asking you what actually happened in the voting booth. What happened in the voting booth? Here am I, from Zadar. I'm following somebody from Knin. I can see he's being given a voting paper. I also want a voting paper. What did you give me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once that person produces his personal identity card --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Answer me. What did you give me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. We gave them nothing. We just made this list in situ. We compiled the list in situ, having seen on the basis of his identity card that he doesn't have the proper place of residence to be entitled to vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And they were happy that they had voted and therefore there was no trouble?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were aware of the fact that they were not entitled to vote. Some of them required explanations but most of them knew this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking you: Were they happy that they had voted and they went away peacefully? You successfully avoided the problem that you were avoiding when you just don't give them an option to vote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were no incidents. There was not a single incident and I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is, were they happy that they had voted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in some way they were. In a way their will would be communicated, and it was communicated in a way, but this was not proper election procedure, it being unlawful for them to vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Anybody knows, anybody knows that when you vote you vote on a ballot paper, and if it's not on the ballot paper the vote is spoiled. We know that, don't we? We all know that. That's a spoiled paper.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. So how can they be happy that they voted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't explain whether they were happy. It is a fact that they didn't get those voting slips, because they were not on the electoral rolls, because they did not have a place of residence that would entitle them to that, which was established having consulted their identity cards. So we told them, if you want to be on the voting list, we can put you on it. You can express your will, but that will not be of bearing on the final results and outcome of the referendum. We told them that, and we didn't encounter any problems. This was just something that we dealt with in our stride. We hadn't been aware that this would in fact occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am. And if you just said to them, sorry ladies and gentlemen, you may not vote because you do not belong to Knin, you would have had problems on your hands, you said. You're sure about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure of it, because these people had covered some 50, 60 or 70 kilometres to come and they would say, we came here to express our wills. And when we explained to them that we couldn't allow them to vote because it was contrary to the law and we wanted a referendum that would be valid according to the law, they acquiesced, because they understood what our problem was. But still they wanted to be seen as having come to express the will of their people. And they knew that we had made a separate list and they saw this as showing that they had exerted this effort to also communicate their will and express their will and they accepted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. You have tried to answer me as best as we can. We can't take the point much further. Thank you. That is the end of my questions. Mr. Milovancevic? Any questions arising from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just one or two, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Madam, isn't it true that as of -- and this is with respect to the questions about which laws applied in the SAO Krajina. Isn't it true that as of the 28th of February, 1991, the laws of the Republic of Croatia did not apply in the SAO Krajina if they conflicted in any way with the laws of the SAO Krajina, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well frankly speaking, I cannot give you a decided answer as to whether there were any laws that were not applied. Over 15 years have passed. I really cannot give you a definite answer at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me put a different, more specific point to you. And if we could actually look at Exhibit 144 in evidence, please. And I would draw your attention to the Article 2 of this decision of the 1st of April, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We need to get the English version on our screen. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In Article 2 in the second paragraph it says: "In accordance with the preceding paragraph of this article as of the adoption of this decision, the constitution of the Republic of Serbia is valid within the territory of the SAO Krajina, and the laws of the Republic of Serbia are applied, as is the constitutional legal system of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." So the answer is, isn't it, that as of the 1st of April, 1991, the constitution of Serbia, the laws of Serbia, and the laws of the Federal Republic, the SFRY, applied in the SAO Krajina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is probably so, according to this decision in which I didn't participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, madam --

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I probably have seen it but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, madam. Why is it probably so? It is so, isn't it? This decision clearly states it.

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And one final question. The reason you took the referendum to Serbia and not to the SFRY is because you, meaning the SAO Krajina, wanted to join with Serbia, right?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're asking me personally, according to what I know, it was always my wish to remain in Yugoslavia and I believe that that wish was shared by the entirety of the Serbian people, to remain in Yugoslavia, and if that should prove to be possible -- impossible, if that should prove to be impossible, then possibly, as part of some other countries that would remain. And I still maintain that position. That was a state in which I and my entire community, irrespective of their nationalities, ethnicities, really lived good lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But madam, the fact is that although you say now that the entirety of the Serbian people wanted to remain in Yugoslavia, in May of 1991, you took that referendum to Serbia and not to the SFRY government. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: LUJBICA VUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we took it to the Assembly of Serbia, which did not accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just a question, Mr. Whiting. Was there a special reason for you to start this questions now, referring to the 28th of February? Or was this a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, it was not a mistake. It is a reference to a document that I have, but it's not in evidence. So I decided simply to expedite and not to pursue it and to focus on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mrs. Vujanic, this brings us to the end of your testimony. The Chamber would like to take this time to thank you very much for coming to testify. We understand you must have your own engagements and your own priorities, and we appreciate the fact that you could take time off your busy schedule to come and testify. Thank you very much for coming, and you are now excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Perhaps there have been some problems because ours is a different criminal procedure compared to this one. Perhaps I amplified on some matters, actually answering more than you asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Once you have been excused, you are not allowed to speak in this. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. We appreciate you coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the next witness will be questioned by Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I have Milan Dragisic, our next witness, ushered in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Dragisic. You may take your seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good evening, Mr. Dragisic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In keeping with the Rules that prevail here, I will now proceed with your examination-in-chief. But before we begin, I must ask you to answer my questions which I will make brief and concise, in a similarly brief and concise way, also to make a very short pause before you start answering a question, to let the interpreters do their job properly. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If my learned friend from the Prosecution has no objection, I would like to lead the witness through his personal history, just to save time. Is it true, Mr. Black, who is going to cross examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and I have no objection to leading through the non-controversial matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Your name is Milan Dragisic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You were born in 1949 in a village called Pribudic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Gracac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That's where you completed primary school in 1964?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After that, the high school in Knin in 1968.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: The same year, you received the call up to do your military service and you were sent to the reserve officer's school in Bilice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Infantry?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: As I read your CV, you do not have to answer "yes", but I will give you a chance at the end to make the necessary corrections, if any. So you completed your military service in 1969 in the rank of junior lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Second Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Until 1974 you worked in Hydro Hidrotechnica enterprise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: In fact I worked there only in 1971 and 1972 and after that I enrolled in a school for applied -- applied computer science.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And you completed it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After that, you went back to Knin and found a job as a teacher of civilian defence. You stayed in that job until 1977, the 1st of April. And on the 1st of April 1977, you found another job in the Territorial Defence of Knin as chief of operations. In the meantime, you read political science in Zagreb and graduated from the Zagreb University, and in 1986 you became Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence of Knin. You remained there until the 25th of July, 1990 when the Assembly, the Municipal Assembly of Knin elected you to be the commander of the TO staff of Knin. And in summer 1991 you were appointed acting Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence of Krajina. From September 1991 until May 1992, you were away on sick leave and treatment --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, if I could object. I'm sorry, I didn't object to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- personal background details but I think now, when we we get into the time frame that's an issue in the case, I think it should be done in the ordinary way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that. I haven't yet finished with the CV, but I do accept that this might be leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So from the 1st of June, 1992, you started teaching at the school for internal affairs in Golubici at a course for Krajina's policemen. In the course of 1993, you were chief at that school until the time when it was transferred to Slovenia, to the town of Erdut. After the school moved, you went to the Ministry of the Interior to work in the state security service as an analyst until the fall of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in 1995. From 1997 until 2004, you worked in the utility's enterprise in Belgrade and you are currently unemployed. Is this personal information correct or do you want to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: No corrections, and nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In 1986, as we can read in your CV, you were appointed Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence of Knin and you remained there until the 25th of July, 1990. Could you please tell me, to whom was the TO staff of Knin subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Stop. There's something that confuses me slightly, Mr. Perovic. On page 84, line 11, you said that the witness was elected -- was appointed, at line 12, was appointed acting Chief of Staff of the TO in Krajina. Now you say in 1986 he was appointed Chief of Staff in Knin now, not in Krajina. Is that the difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is one difference. But there is also a difference in chronology. I'm talking about the period between 1986 and 1990 when the witness occupied the post of Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence of Knin. That is the period I'm referring to now. From 1986 until 1990, he was chief of the staff of the TO Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Perovic. Could you please clarify, because I had thought that he was appointed acting Chief of Staff of the TD of the Krajina in the summer of 1991. Is it the TO or the TD? It's the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall just read for your benefit two sentences which refer to this part of the CV of the witness. In 1986, he became the Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence of Knin, and remained on that post until the 25th of July, 1990. At that time the Assembly of the municipality of Knin elected him to the post of commander of the staff of the Territorial Defence of Knin. So the name has changed. The designation no longer is the chief but the commander of the staff. And in the summer of 1991 he became the acting Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence of the Krajina. Those are the differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. We may not remember all of that detail a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I hope not to confuse you now again. When the witness was elected commander of TO in -- instead of the TO of the Krajina. According to what do you want to explain to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a misunderstanding which is obvious. On the 25th of July, 1990, by decision of the Municipal Assembly of Knin, he was elected to the post of commander of staff of the Territorial Defence of Knin. And the next year, in the summer of 1991, he was appointed acting Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence of the Krajina. Not of Knin, but of the entire Krajina. That is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is that correct, Witness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Dragisic, now we are talking about the period between 1986 and 1990 when you were the Chief of Staff of the Territorial Defence of Knin. So we are discussing that period now. At that time, to whom was the chief of the Territorial Defence of Knin subordinated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: The staff of the TO of the Knin municipality was subordinated to the staff of the communities of the municipality -- of the community of municipalities of Split and that staff, in turn, was subordinated to the staff of the Territorial Defence of Croatia. And the republican staff was subordinated to the General Staff of the JNA, which is to say, to the armed forces of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was such a structure, such an organisation in accordance with the federal and republican regulations on national defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: The laws, both the federal and the republican, that is to say, the law of the Croatian -- the Croatian law on national defence regulated in that manner the question of the subordination of staffs and command, so that there was unity of command, namely singleness of command, being the venue of that being the General Staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is under the constitution and the law on national defence? When I say "constitution", I mean the constitution of Yugoslavia -- what were units of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Units of the Territorial Defence were a component of the armed forces of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When you say a component, I suppose there is another component.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: The other component was the Yugoslav People's Army, namely the first component was the Yugoslav People's Army and the second component was the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the Yugoslav People's Army under the constitution and under the law on national defence was constituted of the Yugoslav People's Army and the units of the Territorial Defence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness and counsel please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you hear that, Mr. Perovic? Stop in between. The interpreters are struggling to keep pace because you overlap with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you clarify, Mr. Perovic, what the expression national defence, exactly means. Law on national defence it says, and this is what the witness also understood, but this just is terminology. What does it mean? National defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you understand the question, Mr. Dragisic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what the law on national defence regulated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: There was a federal as well as a republican law on national defence, and the republican one was in accordance with the federal one. It dealt with all matters, all components of the defence comprising the Yugoslav People's Army, the Territorial Defence, the civil defence as well as all matters pertaining to the defence of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this a satisfactory answer, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was the basic task of Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: The basic task of Territorial Defence units was primarily control of territory, securing of important facilities, and combat against terrorist or sabotage forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the national composition of these units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: The national composition of Territorial Defence units corresponded to the national composition of the population on a given municipality territory or republican territory. For instance, in the municipality of Knin, 92 per cent of them were Serbs, and the -- approximately, that is the number of Serbs in Territorial Defence units. However, there was some villages in which the population was 100 per cent Croatian, and in such villages the Territorial Defence was 100 per cent Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So the national parity principle was applied?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was this national parity principle also applied to the commands of the staffs and of the Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: The principle was as follows: In the units, if the commander was a Serb, the deputy commander would be a Croat. And the permanent composition of the staff employed both Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was -- did the Territorial Defence have its own weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence had its own armourments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Wherever it was possible, they were in the depots of the Yugoslav People's Army, in order for the weapons to be secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So weapons -- the weapons and weaponry of the Territorial Defence of Knin to be very concrete, where were those?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: They were in the Krka depot of the JNA and the quartermaster supplies, I mean the blankets and the uniforms, they were in a depot in a store house on Petra Drapsina street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Could the weapons be taken out from the depots and what was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: The weapons could not be taken out from the depots without observers of a specific procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who was the one who decided on the possible issuance of weapons from the depots?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: The staff of the Territorial Defence would submit a request to the staff of the community of municipalities of Split, which would refer the same to the command of the JNA unit, and it would then allow the weapons to be taken out from the depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the period under review, so we're talking about 1986 to 1990, at the helm of the Territorial Defence of the community of municipalities of Split, was who, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: It was Colonel Ante Marinov, an officer of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What was he by nationality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, what were the arms of the Territorial Defence like? What was -- what were they? What weapons are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: These were primarily older pieces of weaponry that the JNA had actually decommissioned when it was being modernised, and these were M48 rifles. And in the period that we are talking about, they also had automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles. They had hand throws, launchers and a smaller number of mortars. Sixty and 82 millimeter mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To the extent that I am knowledgeable about weapons, are these all infantry weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were all infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just briefly describe for us the command structure of the Territorial Defence until the war, that is from 1986 to 1990. What was the command structure like at that time? Can you explain more specifically?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: The highest organ in the republic was the republican staff of Territorial Defence, and at its helm was General Spegelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. You are speaking about the Territorial Defence of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Where was the seat of the Territorial Defence of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: It was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: To whom was answerable to staff of the Territorial Defence of Croatia under the law?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Under the law it was answerable to the General Staff of the JNA and to the Presidency of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned the name of the commander of the Territorial Defence of Croatia in the period under review. Can you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: It was general Martin Spegelj and after him it was General Novoselic. The Chief of Staff was General Vracarevic. He was a Serb and the two commanders were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under the staff of the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia, what was the structure under it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: After that, we had each community of municipalities had its own staff of communities of municipalities and the second in command, as far as we were concerned, was the staff of the community of municipalities of Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And then following that, the Municipal Staff, the Municipal Staff in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who financed the financial municipal Territorial Defence Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: According to the law on All Peoples Defence, the municipal Territorial Defence Staffs were funded from the budget of the municipality in question and the allocation was, if I remember correctly, 0.40 per cent of the revenues of the budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And just another question for today, because we are about to wrap up for today. According to the command chain, the command line, the Territorial Defence Staff of Knin was subordinated to whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN DRAGISIC
utterances.text: It was subordinated to the staff of the community of municipalities of Split at whose helm was Colonel Marinov.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that we should continue in the morning, because Your Honours, I suppose that we have -- we can call it a day at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are very correct, Mr. Perovic. Let's call it a day and come back at 9 o'clock tomorrow morning. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of September, 2006 at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
